children: By Staff Writer

A safari can offer more than the chance to see wildlife in its natural environment. Done responsibly, a wildlife experience can also help visitors understand the importance of conservation, animal welfare and protecting the ecosystems that support South Africa’s natural heritage.

Wildlife reserves and conservation centres can provide a bridge between tourism and education, giving visitors the opportunity to learn about species, habitats and the challenges involved in protecting them. The Bothongo Rhino & Lion Nature Reserve, located in the Cradle of Humankind, provides one example of how these elements can be incorporated into the visitor experience.
Conservation extends beyond protecting animals
Conservation is often presented through the lens of endangered species and anti-poaching efforts, but the reality is considerably broader.
It involves habitat management, animal welfare, research, education, biodiversity and helping communities and visitors understand the complex relationship between people and wildlife.

Wildlife centres can also play an educational role by giving the public access to animals and information they may not otherwise encounter. At Bothongo Rhino & Lion Nature Reserve, the Wildlife Centre cares for animals that have been rescued, rejected, hand-reared or are undergoing rehabilitation, while giving visitors an opportunity to learn more about their circumstances.
For younger visitors in particular, experiences of this kind can turn an abstract conversation about conservation into something tangible.
Tourism can strengthen connections with nature

South Africa’s wildlife is one of its major natural assets, attracting visitors from around the country and the world. Wildlife tourism can also help keep people connected to the natural environment at a time when many, particularly children, have fewer opportunities to experience nature in their everyday lives.
That connection can extend beyond wildlife itself.

The Bothongo Rhino & Lion Nature Reserve is located within the Cradle of Humankind and includes access to the Bothongo WonderCave, adding a geological dimension to the visitor experience. The cave forms part of the wider UNESCO World Heritage Site, which is recognised for its paleoanthropological significance.

Experiencing wildlife alongside the geological history of the landscape can give visitors a broader understanding of the environment they are exploring, from the animals and ecosystems above ground to the natural history beneath it.
For visitors, this creates an opportunity to slow down, observe and ask questions about animal behaviour, habitats, biodiversity, geology and the history of the landscape.
The experience therefore becomes about more than seeing wildlife. It can help visitors understand the environment in which those animals exist and the natural heritage that surrounds them.
Making education part of the safari experience
The way visitors experience wildlife can influence how they understand conservation.

Guided experiences, self-drives and wildlife centres can all provide opportunities to learn about species and ecosystems, particularly when information is presented alongside direct encounters with animals.

The Bothongo reserve, for example, offers visitors opportunities to encounter a range of wildlife and learn about species that are rarely seen outside protected environments. Its conservation activities also include opportunities to observe vultures, which play an important role in healthy ecosystems.

These experiences demonstrate how wildlife tourism can support conservation awareness. When visitors leave with a better understanding of the animals and environments they have encountered, they may also leave with a stronger appreciation of why those environments need protection.
Choosing wildlife experiences with a purpose
For travellers and families planning a safari, the experience itself can form part of the decision-making process.
Beyond asking which animals they might see, visitors can consider how a destination approaches animal welfare, education, conservation and environmental responsibility.
There is no single way to experience the South African bush, but choosing destinations that incorporate these principles can make a wildlife outing more meaningful.

The value of a safari ultimately extends beyond the photographs visitors take home. By creating opportunities to learn about wildlife, habitats and the wider environment, responsible tourism can help strengthen people's connection to the natural heritage they are visiting.
The most valuable wildlife experience may therefore be one that leaves visitors not only with memories of what they saw, but with a greater understanding of why it needs to be protected.
